faq.a: Argatroban directly prolongs aPTT; dabigatran does not reliably affect aPTT at therapeutic levels.
faq.q: Why is aPTT used to monitor argatroban but not dabigatran?
What is the antidote for dabigatran?

faq.a: No, it is contraindicated; use argatroban or bivalirudin instead.
faq.q: Can dabigatran be used in patients with severe renal failure?

exam: A 68‑year‑old man with atrial fibrillation and CKD stage 3 is started on dabigatran. He develops haematuria. — Discuss monitoring and management of bleeding in renal impairment.
A patient with suspected HIT is started on argatroban. His aPTT rises above target. — Explain how to adjust dosing and why aPTT is used.
A 55‑year‑old woman on dabigatran presents with sudden headache and vomiting. Imaging shows subarachnoid haemorrhage. — Outline emergency steps and the role of idarucizumab.
A 45‑year‑old man with DVT is switched from LMWH to dabigatran. He is on a herbal anticoagulant. — Identify potential interactions and how to manage.
A patient with atrial fibrillation is on warfarin with INR 3.5. The doctor wants to switch to a DTI. — Discuss advantages and disadvantages of switching.
A 60‑year‑old man with VTE is on dabigatran. He is admitted with sepsis and acute kidney injury. — Explain how to adjust therapy and monitor.
A 70‑year‑old woman with atrial fibrillation is on dabigatran but has a history of GI bleeding. — Discuss risk assessment and alternative anticoagulation.
A 50‑year‑old man with HIT is treated with bivalirudin. He develops thrombosis. — Explain why thrombosis can still occur and what to do.
ai.title: Direct Thrombin Inhibitors
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Direct thrombin inhibitors block thrombin directly, preventing fibrin formation. They are used for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. They have predictable pharmacokinetics and limited monitoring.

b: No need for routine INR monitoring
sections.p: Direct thrombin inhibitors (DTIs) are anticoagulants that bind thrombin (factor IIa) irreversibly or reversibly, blocking its activity on fibrinogen and platelet activation. Diagnosis of a need for DTI is clinical: patients with atrial fibrillation, VTE, or HIT requiring anticoagulation.
Severity is not staged by the drug itself but by the underlying condition: e.g., VTE (DVT/PE), atrial fibrillation, or HIT. Clinical staging uses Wells score for VTE and CHA₂DS₂-VASc for AF.

b: Deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism

sections.p: Patients on DTIs are usually asymptomatic unless bleeding occurs. Bleeding signs include bruising, hematuria, melena, or haemorrhagic shock. In HIT, thrombosis and thrombocytopenia appear 5–10 days after heparin exposure.
Key investigations guide initiation and monitoring.

t.b: Determines dosing and choice of DTI; dabigatran is renally cleared
Screen for HIT; a drop >50% suggests HIT
Used to monitor argatroban or bivalirudin; should be 1.5–2.5× baseline

sections.p: Bleeding is the main danger. Watch for signs of intracranial haemorrhage, GI bleeding, and haemorrhagic shock. In HIT, new thrombosis or skin necrosis are red flags.

b: Use argatroban in liver disease (metabolised hepatically)
Use bivalirudin in renal impairment (renal clearance)
sections.p: Stop heparin immediately if HIT suspected. Switch to a DTI: argatroban or bivalirudin for IV use; dabigatran for oral therapy. Monitor renal function and coagulation as needed. Reversal with idarucizumab is available for dabigatran.
Regular review of renal function, drug interactions, and adherence. Counsel patients on bleeding precautions and avoid NSAIDs. For AF, reassess CHA₂DS₂‑VASc annually.
Other DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) and warfarin. Unlike warfarin, DTIs do not require INR monitoring.
aPTT may be normal in dabigatran use; renal impairment can falsely elevate dabigatran levels. Platelet count may be normal early in HIT.
